native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among black NLSY79 respondents, jailing between 1985 and 1994 is associated with persistent wealth loss whose form depends on baseline economic position (1985 wealth tier as income proxy, since no income variable exists): those starting with little/no wealth (<≈$9,200) were trapped at zero net worth (median 1996 wealth $0 vs $5,000–$16,000 for never-jailed peers; 58–67% of jailed ending at ≤$0 in tiers 0–2 vs 21–30% of never-jailed; black men 56–67% vs 18–31%), while those starting in the top tier (>≈$24,900) avoided the zero trap (30.3% vs 21.1% at ≤$0) but took the largest absolute hits (median 1985→1996 change −$9,500 vs +$6,900). Regression-estimated jailed penalties rise with baseline tier (≈−$34k to ≈−$65k, all p<0.001); effect concentrated among black men (113/124 jailed) and in the post-window 1990→1996 period; robust to duplicate retention; association, not causation.
native_result.WorkflowB: Load & validate CSV (12,013×6, 0 missing, schema verified) → deduplicate (10,114 unique; black n=2,465, jailed 124) → define Δ_early/Δ_late/Δ_total (primary: 1990→1996 and 1985→1996) → baseline-1985 wealth tiers (≤0; ≤$5,400; ≤$9,200; >$24,899) as income proxy → tier×jailed median-trajectory tables for black-all/black-males (primary), black-females (small-n caveat), duplicates-retained sensitivity, white-male context → OLS with HC3 SEs: d_total and signed-log(d_total) ~ tier×ever_jailed+sex → export 5 tables and quantify natural-language hypothesis with verified percentages.

sub_hypo.text: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
sub_hypo.context: Black individuals in the National Longitudinal Study of Youth's 1979 cohort.
sub_hypo.relations: Incarceration negatively impacts wealth, but this negative impact may be smaller for the high-income group than for individuals at lower wealth ranges.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.

sub_hypo.text: Among black NLSY79 respondents starting with little or no wealth in 1985 (up to approximately $9,200), jailing between 1985 and 1994 was associated with a persistent zero-net-worth trap: median 1996 wealth was $0 versus $5,000–$16,000 for never-jailed peers, and 58–67% ended with wealth at or below $0 versus 21–30% of never-jailed peers.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLSY79 respondents in baseline 1985 wealth tiers 0–2 (≤$0, up to $5,400, and up to $9,200); baseline wealth serves as an income proxy because no income variable exists.
sub_hypo.relations: Within low baseline wealth tiers, jailing is associated with lower median 1996 wealth and a higher proportion ending at nonpositive net worth; association, not causation.

sub_hypo.text: Among black men starting in the low 1985 wealth tiers, 56–67% of those jailed between 1985 and 1994 ended with wealth at or below $0 in 1996, compared with 18–31% of never-jailed peers.
sub_hypo.context: Male black NLSY79 respondents in baseline 1985 wealth tiers 0–2, extending through approximately $9,200.
sub_hypo.relations: Jailing is associated with a higher prevalence of nonpositive 1996 wealth among black men with low baseline wealth.

sub_hypo.text: Black NLSY79 respondents in the top 1985 wealth tier avoided the low-tier zero trap but experienced the largest absolute wealth losses associated with jailing: 30.3% of jailed respondents versus 21.1% of never-jailed peers ended with nonpositive wealth, while median 1985–1996 wealth change was −$9,500 versus +$6,900.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLSY79 respondents with baseline 1985 wealth above $24,899, approximately $24,900.
sub_hypo.relations: The form of the jailing–wealth association depends on baseline wealth: the top tier has less zero trapping than low tiers but the largest absolute wealth hits.

sub_hypo.text: Among black NLSY79 respondents, regression-estimated jailed wealth penalties increased in magnitude with baseline wealth tier, from approximately −$34,000 to −$65,000, with all p-values below 0.001.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLSY79 respondents; baseline 1985 wealth tiers used as an income proxy; OLS models with HC3 standard errors and adjustment for sex.
sub_hypo.relations: Baseline wealth tier interacts with jailing status in models of 1985–1996 wealth change and its signed-log transformation; estimated negative jailed penalties become larger at higher tiers.

sub_hypo.text: The association between jailing and persistent wealth loss among black NLSY79 respondents was concentrated among men, who accounted for 113 of 124 jailed respondents, and in the 1990–1996 period; it remained robust when duplicates were retained.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLSY79 respondents, with primary analyses of all black respondents and black men, a small-sample caveat for black women, and duplicate-retention sensitivity analysis.
sub_hypo.relations: The negative jailing–wealth association is concentrated among black men and in 1990–1996 rather than the earlier period, and is robust to retaining duplicate records; it is not a causal claim.
